source_text: Quid iam de illa loquar potentia. qua intellegitur ueritas, qua istis ipsis, quae de corporis sensu haustae figurantur. imaginibus sese pro ueritate obponentibus magna uiuacitate resistitur? qua uidetur aliam uerbi gratia ueram esse Karthaginem, aliam, quam cogitans fingit et pro suo arbitrio tota facilitate conmutat, ex eadem uenire facilitate innumerabiles mundos, in quibus Epicuri cogitatio innumerabiliter peregrinata est, et, ne multa consecter, ex eadem uenire facilitate istam terram lucis per spatia infinita diffusam et quinque antra gentis tenebrarum cum habitatoribus suis. in quibus Manichaei phantasmata ueritatis sibi nomen ausa sunt usurpare. quid est ergo haec potentia. quae ista discernit? profecto quantacumque sit, et his omnibus maior est et sine ulla tali rerum imaginatione cogitatur. huic inueni spatia, si potes. hanc diffunde per locos, hanc infinitae molis tumore distende. profecto si bene cogitas, non potes. quicquid enim tale tibi occurrerit, iudicas ipsa cogitatione secari posse per partes facisque ibi aliam partem minorem, aliam maiorem. quantum placet; illud autem ipsum, quo ista iudicas, cernis esse supra ista, non loci altitudine, sed potentiae dignitate.
thought_title: The mind's judging power surpasses all spatial images
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the mind is not spread out through space, and now turns to the power by which it judges truth and resists false images, including Mani's land of light.
pass_a_gloss: What now shall I say about that power by which truth is understood, by which resistance is made with great liveliness to these very images, which are formed from what has been drawn from the sense of the body, when they set themselves against truth in place of truth? By which power it is seen that one Carthage, for example, is true, and another Carthage, which the mind imagines in thinking and changes with total ease according to its own judgment, and that from the same ease come innumerable worlds, in which the thought of Epicurus wandered innumerably, and, so that I do not pursue many things, that from the same ease comes that land of light spread through infinite spaces and the five caves of the nation of darkness with their inhabitants, in which the fantasies of Mani have dared to usurp for themselves the name of truth. What therefore is this power which discerns these things? Certainly, however great it may be, it is both greater than all these things and is thought of without any such imagining of things. Find spaces for this power, if you can. Spread this power through places, distend this power with the swelling of an infinite mass. Certainly, if you think well, you cannot. For whatever such thing occurs to you, you judge by that very thinking that it can be cut into parts, and you make there one part smaller, another larger, as much as pleases; but that very thing itself, by which you judge these things, you discern to be above these things, not by height of place, but by dignity of power.

choices.why: The glossary does not fix this term, but 'power' preserves the sense of a faculty or capacity of the mind that Augustine contrasts with spatial extension.
The glossary requires 'fantasies' for phantasmata, referring to images formed from bodily sense experience that Mani mistook for reality.
The glossary requires 'land of light' for terra lucis, Mani's eternal realm of God.
The glossary fixes 'land of darkness' for terra tenebrarum, but here the source uses gens tenebrarum, so 'nation of darkness' preserves the distinct term while staying close to the glossary's sense.

choices.english: with the swelling of an infinite mass
choices.why: This renders the spatial metaphor literally, preserving Augustine's image of distending the mind as if it were a bodily mass.
rejected: with the bulk of an infinite mass
with the tumor of infinite size

choices.why: This keeps the contrast between spatial height and the non-spatial superiority of the judging power, preserving the literal sense of dignitas.
rejected: by the worth of its power

pass_b_english: Why should I speak now of that power by which truth is understood—the power that resists with great vigor those very images drawn from the senses of the body and shaped in the mind, when they set themselves up in place of the truth? By this power one sees that the real Carthage is one thing, and another is the Carthage the mind imagines and changes with total ease as it pleases. From that same ease come the countless worlds through which the thought of Epicurus wandered without number. And, not to pursue many examples, from that same ease comes that land of light spread through infinite spaces, and the five caves of the nation of darkness with their inhabitants, in which the Manichaeans' fantasies have dared to claim for themselves the name of truth. What then is this power that discerns these things? However great it may be, it is greater than all of them, and it is thought without any such imagining of things. Find spaces for it, if you can. Spread it through places. Distend it with the swelling of an infinite mass. If you think rightly, you cannot. For whatever of that kind occurs to you, you judge by that very thought that it can be cut into parts, and you make one part smaller there, another larger, as much as you please. But that very thing by which you judge these things, you see is above them—not by height of place, but by dignity of power.

problems.why: "Manichaei" is genitive plural "of the Manichaeans," not genitive singular "of Mani"; the fantasies belong to Mani's followers collectively.
problems.ruling: Manichaei is genitive plural 'of the Manichaeans,' not 'of Mani'; attributes fantasies to wrong subject.

fixed: Changed 'Mani's fantasies' to 'the Manichaeans' fantasies' because 'Manichaei' is genitive plural, referring to Mani's followers collectively, not to Mani himself.

problems.quote: the power that resists with great vigor those very images drawn from the senses of the body and shaped in the mind, when they set themselves against the truth
problems.source_quote: qua istis ipsis, quae de corporis sensu haustae figurantur. imaginibus sese pro ueritate obponentibus magna uiuacitate resistitur
problems.why: Source says images set themselves up in place of/for truth (pro ueritate), not against it; 'against' reverses the sense of opposition vs. substitution.
problems.fix: ...resists with great vigor those very images, drawn from bodily sense and formed in the mind, that set themselves up in place of the truth?

edits.old: when they set themselves against the truth
edits.new: when they set themselves up in place of the truth

fixed: mistranslation real: fixed - source 'sese pro ueritate obponentibus' means setting themselves up in place of truth, not against truth.

last_rejected.why: Manichaei is singular genitive: 'Mani's fantasies,' not 'the Manichaeans' fantasies.'
last_rejected.ruling: Manichaei is plural genitive ('of the Manichaeans'), not singular; 'Manichaeans' fantasies' is correct.

last_rejected.quote: the Manichaeans' fantasies have dared to claim for themselves the name of truth
last_rejected.source_quote: Manichaei phantasmata ueritatis sibi nomen ausa sunt usurpare
last_rejected.why: Manichaei is genitive singular with neuter ausa sunt: the fantasies are Mani's, not the Manichaeans'.
last_rejected.fix: Mani's fantasies have dared to usurp for themselves the name of truth
last_rejected.ruling: Manichaei is probably genitive singular (Mani's), but 'Manichaeans' fantasies' still conveys the same target and reference; the change is minor, not a meaning-altering error.
